paras: The attempted lynching of Lawyer Tobias was a mob pursuit in southeastern Kansas on August 12, 1920, after Tobias, a young Black man, was accused of shooting Howard Thomas, a white cement manufacturer, at Fort Scott. Cars of armed Fort Scott men chased the officers who moved Tobias to Pittsburg, Kansas, and then to the jail at Joplin, Missouri. Tobias was later convicted of the shooting and sent to the penitentiary.

Tobias had come to Fort Scott about three weeks earlier, reportedly from Mississippi with his mother, and worked for the Fort Scott Hydraulic Cement company, of which Thomas was secretary-treasurer. According to a Fort Scott dispatch, the shooting late on August 11 followed an argument over Tobias's pay; Thomas was hit five times but was expected to recover.

A mob said to number several thousand gathered at Fort Scott, and between 100 and 200 automobiles filled with men left early on August 12 to search for Tobias. The Fort Scott dispatch reported that members of the mob had expressed the intention of hanging him if he was found. Half a dozen of Thomas's former military comrades caught Tobias at Garland, ten miles southeast of Fort Scott, after watching for him all night, and Sheriff Armour of Bourbon County arrested him.

Armour slipped away from the gathering crowd and reached Pittsburg, in Crawford County, with his prisoner that morning. When a report came from Arma, eight miles north, that three cars of men displaying guns and ropes had passed through, the sheriff hurried out of Pittsburg with Tobias around 11 o'clock. The pursuers were then said to be heading for Girard, the Crawford County seat, where Sheriff Milt Gould removed several Black prisoners from the jail.

Shortly after noon the Crawford County sheriff and the Pittsburg police chief delivered Tobias to the Joplin jail, where police chief Myers kept a car and officers with riot guns ready to move him again if a mob appeared.

Tobias, called "Lawrence Tobias" in a later Fort Scott dispatch, was convicted of shooting Thomas, described as his employer, and sentenced to the penitentiary for one to ten years. The sentence was briefly in doubt because Tobias, his mother and a Louisiana sheriff said he was 14, too young for the penitentiary under Kansas law. Physicians judged him at least 22, the court accepted their opinion, and he was sent to the penitentiary on September 6. No report of any arrest or charge against members of the mob appears in the coverage.

White papers from Tennessee to Oregon carried Associated Press dispatches from Pittsburg and Joplin on August 12 and 13, under headlines such as "Negro Who Shot Man Moved To Avoid Lynching" (Omaha Daily Bee) and "Protecting Negro From Lynching Bee" (Salem Capital Journal). The Topeka State Journal combined dispatches from three towns into the fullest account, and its headlines, like the Moscow, Idaho, Daily Star-Mirror's "NEGRO MURDERER," called Tobias a "Murderer" and "Slayer" though Thomas was expected to recover. The Daily Ardmoreite in Oklahoma took a different tone, headlining its report "Bleeding Kansas Mob Would Lynch a Poor Unfortunate Black for Shooting a White."

The Black press took up the episode weeks later through an Associated Negro Press item dated September 3, printed by the Tulsa Star as "This Sheriff Was No Wooley" and by the Phoenix Tribune as "Kansas Sheriff Foils Mob Bent On Committing Violence To His Prisoner." The item credited Sheriff Clarence Armour with foiling "a big Fort Scott mob bent on lynching a Negro" and added the prisoner's own claim, absent from the white reports, that he had shot in self-defense.

White reports traced the shooting to an argument over pay, while the ANP item reported Tobias's statement that he fired in self-defense. The ANP item also spoke of "the killing of a white man" on "last Saturday night" and named Arma as the place of safekeeping, unlike the same-day wire reports of a wounding on August 11 and a removal to Pittsburg and Joplin. Names varied as well: the prisoner appeared as "Lawyer," "Lawler" and "Lawrence" Tobias, and the sheriff as "Charles" and "Clarence" Armour. His age was given as about 18 by the Fort Scott dispatch, 14 by his family and at least 22 by physicians.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Lawyer Tobias
bases: A mob from Fort Scott said to number thousands pursued the officers holding Tobias with the stated intent to hang him, and he was moved across the state line to escape it (A1, A3, A19).

A crowd of hundreds to thousands, acting without authority to punish Tobias for the shooting of Thomas, hunted him with guns and ropes (A1, A3), but officers kept him out of its reach and he was later tried and sentenced (A13, A20); no one was killed, so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

The Topeka State Journal's Fort Scott and Pittsburg dispatches (A1), the Associated Press reports (A3, A13) and the Associated Negro Press item (A19) agree that a Fort Scott mob pursued the prisoner and that officers moved him to escape it.

accounts.gist: Tobias shot Thomas after an argument over his pay; a mob of thousands formed and pursued the sheriff by car with guns and ropes intending to hang him, and he was taken to Joplin.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press
accounts.gist: Sheriff Armour foiled a big Fort Scott mob by taking the prisoner to Arma; the prisoner says he shot the man in self-defense.

accounts.label: Fort Scott court report
accounts.gist: Tobias was convicted and sentenced to one to ten years; the court accepted physicians' view that he was at least 22 over his family's claim that he was 14.

framing.detail: The Topeka State Journal headlined 'MOBS HUNT FOR FT. SCOTT NEGRO' and 'LYNCHERS IN AUTOMOBILES' but called Tobias 'Murderer' and 'Slayer' though its text said Thomas would likely recover.
The Daily Ardmoreite headlined 'BLEEDING KANSAS MOB WOULD LYNCH A POOR UNFORTUNATE BLACK FOR SHOOTING A WHITE'.
AP Joplin and Pittsburg dispatches ran under headlines such as 'NEGRO MURDERER', 'Negro Slayer Is Moved in Fear of Lynching Attempt' and 'Protecting Negro From Lynching Bee'.
The ANP item praised the sheriff ('This Sheriff Was No Wooley', 'Kansas Sheriff Foils Mob') and added the prisoner's self-defense claim.

record_check.dossier: Not taken from custody: officers kept Tobias ahead of the mob and lodged him at Joplin; the Girard jail was emptied of other Black prisoners before the pursuers could arrive

record_check.record: pursuers went on to Girard, where the prisoner was removed from the jail
record_check.dossier: Tobias was never at Girard; Sheriff Gould removed several other Black prisoners there as a precaution, and Tobias was taken from Pittsburg to Joplin
Most reports say 'Lawyer Tobias'; also 'Lawler' and 'Lawrence'

Armed gathering, pursuit and threat by the mob; the 'seizure' was his capture by Thomas's ex-comrades and arrest by the sheriff, and the 'shooting' was the shooting of Thomas of which Tobias was accused, not mob acts
An unnamed mob of Fort Scott men in automobiles
Tobias convicted and sentenced to one to ten years in the penitentiary, sent September 6

info: Thomas was shot on the night of Wednesday, August 11, 1920; the mob pursuit took place on the morning of August 12
Shooting at Fort Scott; capture at Garland; pursuit toward Pittsburg, Arma, Girard and Mulberry, Kansas; prisoner lodged at Joplin, Missouri
Lawyer Tobias (also 'Lawler', 'Lawrence'), a Black man said to be about 18, recently arrived from Mississippi (or Louisiana), target of the mob
Charged with shooting and wounding Howard Thomas, secretary-treasurer of the Fort Scott Hydraulic Cement company and his employer, after an argument over his pay
An unnamed mob of Fort Scott men in automobiles; Thomas's former service comrades captured Tobias before the sheriff took him
Sentenced to the penitentiary for one to ten years and sent there September 6
